document.title: Response of Advanced Energy United to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s Answer to the Show Cause Order

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. et al.                                             
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities  
 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
v.  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
 
 
 
 
 
Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 
 
 
AD24-11-000 
 
 
EL25-20-000 
(Consolidated) 
 
 
 
 
 
RESPONSE OF ADVANCED ENERGY UNITED 
 
 
Pursuant to the Ordering Paragraph (D) of the Show Cause Order issued by the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”)1 and Rule 212 of the Rules of 
Practice and Procedure of the Commission, Advanced Energy United (“United”)2 submits this 
response to the Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”)3 to the Show Cause Order.  
 
 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C et al 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025) (“Show Cause Order”). 
2 Advanced Energy United is a national association of businesses that are making the energy we use secure, 
clean and affordable. Advanced Energy United is the only industry association in the United States that represents 
the full range of advanced energy technologies and services, both grid-scale and distributed. Advanced energy 
includes energy efficiency, demand response, energy storage, wind, solar, hydro, nuclear, electric vehicles, and 
more. The comments expressed in this filing represent the position of Advanced Energy United but may not 
represent the views of any particular member. 
3 “Answer of PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.” FERC Docket EL25-49-000 March 23, 2025 (“PJM Answer”).

2 
I. 
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
The issue of co-location of large load and generation represents an emerging and 
strategically important development in the evolution of the electric grid. Data centers that hold 
important, sensitive data and support growing artificial intelligence capabilities run applications 
that need large amounts of power to fuel the economy and provide national security. Advanced 
manufacturing facilities that support economic development and onshoring of critical supply 
chains will also require access to reliable, affordable power to compete in a global economy. Co-
location arrangements offer the potential for increased reliability and faster interconnection to the 
grid, but their rapid emergence and different configurations are raising concerns about the 
potential for compromised resource adequacy, reliability, and resiliency. Commission direction 
is critical to bring clarity to this pressing issue, and the Commission has placed appropriate 
attention and urgency on co-location through the Show Cause Order and the Technical 
Conference convened last November.4 United agrees with PJM that the industry needs guidance, 
and urges the Commission to act quickly to reduce regulatory uncertainty and allow large loads 
and generation to interconnect to the grid in a fast and efficient manner while avoiding cost shifts 
to other customers and preserving or even bolstering reliability.  
The Commission should direct PJM to take further action in its evaluation of its Tariffs, 
which include the Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”), Operating Agreement (“OA”), 
and Reliability Assurance Agreement (“RA”). In its Answer, PJM set forth eight variations on 
co-location arrangement structure, of which only three are currently available under PJM’s 
 
4 “Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities” FERC Docket No AD24-11-000, Commissioner Led 
Technical Conference on November 1, 2024. (“Technical Conference”)

3 
existing tariffs.5 PJM rescinded its guidance document, which had been issued as an “initial 
attempt to provide limited guidance after over a year’s worth of unfruitful stakeholder 
discussions.”6  Although PJM blames a lack of stakeholder consensus for the lack of clarity in 
this guidance document,7 continued stakeholder discussion is likely the best approach to work 
through the nuanced considerations of the different co-location configurations and their 
implications for cost allocation, planning, and resource adequacy. Commission guidance—
providing a roadmap and a clear timeline toward a Federal Power Act Section 205 filing from 
PJM— would focus PJM and its stakeholders around a set of solutions and ensure a clear 
pathway for more co-location arrangements under PJM’s tariffs.        
Although this proceeding is focused on PJM and the PJM transmission owners, the 
growing demand for co-location opportunities extends beyond PJM’s boundaries to all regions of 
the United States within FERC’s jurisdiction. A one-size-fits-all solution may not result in 
optimal outcomes—each region of the country has unique reliability challenges and market 
structures; each large customer has different load requirements, generation preferences, and 
operational flexibility; and potential co-location arrangements and technology solutions are 
evolving quickly. After initially resolving some of the key questions regarding co-location in the 
PJM region and gathering pertinent information from the Commissioner-led Technical 
Conference on Meeting the Challenge of Resource Adequacy,8 FERC could issue broad guidance 
but require each transmission provider to independently demonstrate that it addresses co-location 
 
5 Id at Exhibit A.  
6 PJM Answer at 33.  
7 Id. 
8 Meeting the Challenge of Resource Adequacy in Regional Transmission Organization and Independent System 
Operator Regions, Docket No. AD25-7-000 (supplemental notice of agenda issued Apr. 3, 2025).

4 
of large loads and generation in a just and reasonable manner. Specifically, United urges the 
Commission to direct all jurisdictional transmission providers in FERC Order No. 1000 
transmission planning regions to either demonstrate that their open access transmission tariffs 
remain just and reasonable in light of the growing demand for co-location, or submit Federal 
Power Act Section 205 filings that specifically address co-location of large loads and generation. 
Regardless of how the Commission proceeds in the above-captioned dockets, it should 
move quickly and decisively. Reducing regulatory uncertainty and allowing for flexibility in how 
co-location arrangements are treated in wholesale markets should be foremost in the 
Commission’s consideration.   
II. 
COLOCATION AND THE BROADER ENERGY LANDSCAPE 
In its 2024 Long-Term Reliability Assessment, the North American Electric Reliability 
Corporation (“NERC”) found that most of the North American bulk power system faces 
mounting resource adequacy challenges over the next 10 years.9 The assessment found that 
demand growth is higher than any point in the past two decades; specifically citing the size of 
data centers and the speed at which they can connect to the electric grid.10 This is a serious 
challenge for PJM and other transmission providers across the country. These new loads are 
large and can be built quickly. In 2023, data centers consumed 4.4% of total US electricity; this 
number has nearly tripled from 2014.11 Data centers can be built in 18-24 months,12 which 
 
9 NERC, 2024 Long-Term Reliability Assessment (December 2024), at 6. 
10 Id at 31.  
11 Shehabi, A., Smith, S.J., Hubbard, A., Newkirk, A., Lei, N., Siddik, M.A.B., Holecek, B., Koomey, J., Masanet, 
E., Sartor, D. 2024. “2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report” Lawrence Berkeley National 
Laboratory, Berkeley, California at page 52. 
12 Stack Infrastructure, “How speed-to-market is transforming data center design and construction,” (Nov. 25, 2020), 
available at https://www.stackinfra.com/resources/thought-leadership/how-speed-to-market-is-transforming-data-
center-design-and-construction/.

5 
allows limited lead time for system planners to prepare for these large additions to the market. 
But finding solutions that allow these loads and the resources that serve them to connect quickly 
and reliably is an economic and national security imperative. Moreover, meeting the challenge 
will unlock the opportunity to deliver grid reliability and affordability benefits that large, high-
load factor demand can unleash.    
Efficiently meeting the demand from new large loads while also maintaining reliability 
and affordability for existing customers requires well-functioning markets and planning 
processes that can fairly and cost-effectively accommodate growing demand for electricity. 
Through recent rulemakings, the Commission has developed tools to increase integration of 
Distributed Energy Resources (“DER”),13 speed the interconnection of generation and storage to 
the grid,14 and improve transmission planning.15 In addition, Dynamic Line Ratings (“DLR”) are 
already being investigated by the Commission, with dozens of comments and reply comments 
filed in support of further Commission action.16 Other alternative transmission technologies 
(“ATT”), such as advanced conductors and energy management systems, can help to enhance the 
reliability, efficiency and flexibility of the electric grid. Robust implementation and/or 
finalization of these new rules by the Commission and transmission providers is critical to ensure 
that reliability and national security needs are being met.  
Co-located load is an issue in part because FERC Orders No. 2222, 2023 and 1920 are 
not yet fully in place to bring about the needed change to optimize DER participation, 
 
13172 FERC ¶ 61,247 (2020) (FERC Order No. 2222). 
14 184 FERC ¶ 61,054 (2023) (FERC Order No. 2023). 
15 189 FERC ¶ 61,126 (2024) (FERC Order No. 1920). 
16 “Implementation of Dynamic Line Rating” FERC Docket AD22-5.

6 
interconnect generation to the wholesale electric grid at a rate fast enough to meet growing 
demand and build out the transmission system proactively and cost-effectively to meet future 
reliability needs. As Brian George, US Federal Lead for Google, stated during the November 1, 
2024 Technical Conference, co-locating load with large generation facilities is “the result of 
market inadequacy.”17 Co-located load is a manifestation of a broader set of challenges that the 
Commission has already been working to address. The Commission must continue to focus on 
the larger issues causing resource adequacy shortages across the country, including through the 
upcoming Resource Adequacy Technical Conference.18  
Nevertheless, within this broader context of ongoing regulatory reforms and rapid load 
growth, co-location presents an important tool to bring online new load and new generation in a 
fast and efficient way. Co-location has emerged out of a necessity for data centers and other 
large loads to interconnect quickly to the electric grid, offering a pathway to smooth the 
integration of large loads into the grid by resolving the disconnect between grid planning and 
infrastructure construction timelines (which are generally slow) and data center and advanced 
manufacturing deployment timelines (which can be very fast). Co-location should not be used to 
avoid or shift costs from the large loads to other consumers, and indeed large energy users have 
confirmed that their interest in co-location is motivated by speed to market, not opportunities for 
cost savings.19  
 
17 George, B (November 1, 2024) “Commissioner-led Technical Conference Regarding Large Loads Co- 
Located at Generating Facilities” (2:32:40) https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/events/commissioner-led-
technicalconference-regarding-large-loads-co-located. 
18 Meeting the Challenge of Resource Adequacy in Regional Transmission Organization and Independent System 
Operator Regions, Docket No. AD25-7-000 (supplemental notice of agenda issued Apr. 3, 2025). 
19 Post-Conference Comments of Google LLC in AD24-11, at 3 (“co-location is driven by a need to secure sufficient 
resources to ensure our timely growth, not a desire to avoid infrastructure costs.” Emphasis original.) Post-
Conference Comments of the Clean Energy Buyers Alliance in AD24-11, at 10.

7 
While demand for co-location and the variety of co-location arrangements customers are 
seeking have increased rapidly, co-location itself is nothing new. Large energy users have been 
co-locating with generation both in front of and behind the meter for decades, deploying 
technologies such as solar, wind, combined heat and power, and battery storage. These resources 
provide additional reliability and resiliency and help customers to control costs and (if 
applicable) meet sustainability goals. Customers have pursued these arrangements in many 
different jurisdictions, including traditional vertically integrated utilities and competitive 
generation markets, and through different means, including net metering agreements and special 
commercial or industrial tariffs. The success of these existing co-location agreements should not 
be disrupted and can be viewed as a starting point for further innovation. Competitive markets 
are helping to bring new products and services as well. As Marjorie Phillips of LS Power stated 
during the Technical Conference, “let markets work…[they] can be very innovative.”20  
Load growth is an economic opportunity, but it may present a crisis if we fail to mobilize 
all available solutions to meet it. This means continuing the Commission’s ongoing efforts to 
improve regional market and planning processes, pursuing additional reforms to meet broader 
market and grid needs, and simultaneously taking steps to ensure that a variety of flexible co-
location arrangements are available as another viable path to accommodate new large loads. A 
comprehensive approach that includes clear and fair rules for co-location will allow us to meet 
load growth cost-effectively, reliably, and in a manner that is fair to all customers. 
 
 
20 Phillips, M.,(November 1, 2024) “Commissioner-led Technical Conference Regarding Large Loads Co-Located 
at Generating Facilities” (2:20:22) https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/events/commissioner-led-
technicalconference-regarding-large-loads-co-located

8 
III. 
PERSPECTIVES ON CO-LOCATION ISSUES 
A. The Commission Should Act Within its Jurisdiction to Facilitate Fair Co-
Location Options While Preserving State Jurisdiction Over Retail Issues 
As FERC recognized in its Show Cause Order, there is a shared responsibility between 
states and the Commission with respect to service to co-located load and generation. While 
FERC, PJM, or another RTO/ISO cannot infringe on a states’ ability to regulate retail sales of 
energy and distribution services to retail load, the Federal Power Act does grant FERC 
jurisdiction over transmission service and wholesale energy sales in interstate commerce.21 This 
jurisdiction gives FERC and PJM an important role in the co-location of large loads and 
generation.   
States, along with RTOs/ISOs, are grappling with the issues of increasing demand and 
retirement of existing generation without new resources replacing them fast enough. Solutions to 
these issues must be weighed against state policies and goals pertaining to economic 
development, generation mix, energy affordability, and other priorities. Some states have opened 
proceedings, developed special tariffs, or are taking other steps to address issues related to the 
rapid rise in large load additions.22 These developments at the state level are emergent, and are 
subject to change at the discretion of the relevant state regulatory authorities. 
Given the evolving nature of this issue and the fact that each state has a different 
regulatory structure and faces different issues and circumstances, there must be flexibility in any 
tariff changes put forward by PJM to accommodate states’ different and evolving regulatory 
frameworks with respect to large loads. In its Answer, PJM observes that not all co-location 
 
21 16 U.S.C. §§ 824(a)-(c).   
22 See, e.g., Utility Commission of Nevada, Docket No. 24-05022, Order Approving Stipulation (March 11, 2025); ” 
Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, Cause No. 46097, Order of the Commission, Settlement Agreement.

9 
options outlined as potential solutions will be available in all states.23 State regulatory structures 
and state laws may prevent or encourage any of the arrangements that are listed in PJM’s 
Answer; this will differ across the PJM footprint and may change over time. PJM’s observation 
that not all options will be available in all states does not warrant excluding any of the options—
in fact, it argues for broad availability of options in PJM’s tariff so that states in the PJM region 
can decide whether changes to state law are needed to either expand or constrain access to co-
location options, according to state-specific circumstances and policy goals. This is consistent 
with long-standing Commission precedent, whereby broadly applicable rules are crafted with 
sufficient flexibility to accommodate state differences.24 The more flexibility granted within 
PJM’s tariff to facilitate different kinds of co-location arrangements, the more discretion states 
will have to determine how to best address co-location within their jurisdiction, including 
whether to pursue changes to their laws and policies in light of co-location arrangements made 
possible under PJM’s tariff.  
The Commission and PJM should also keep in mind that states play a pivotal role in who 
pays for transmission costs, as they are responsible for the allocation of costs at the retail level. 
Thus, while the Commission and PJM have the authority to determine wholesale costs that 
would be allocated to load serving entities, states still have authority to determine how the costs 
are distributed among customer classes, and some states have already taken action to adjust the 
allocation of transmission costs in response to the influx of large loads.25   
 
23 PJM Answer at 29. 
24 172 FERC ¶ 61,041 at P 36, Order No. 1920-A at P 275, 345, 352, Order No. 2222 at P 18. 
25 See Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission, Cause No. 46097, Order of the Commission, Settlement Agreement 
Attachment A.

10 
Any co-location scenario inherently involves a sharing of jurisdictional responsibility, 
and any tariff or rule changes resulting from this proceeding must reflect the authority that is 
granted to the different regulatory bodies. Codifying a range of co-location options in PJM’s 
tariffs will give states flexibility within their jurisdictional purview to encourage, constrain, or 
disallow different co-location options according to their priorities and circumstances.     
B. PJM Tariffs Regarding Co-Location Agreements Do Not Provide Sufficient 
Clarity and Consistency 
PJM states that its tariffs are just and reasonable26 while also acknowledging that 
clarifications and enhancements could be made to accommodate additional co-location 
configurations.27 PJM also recognizes that only three of the co-location eight scenarios it 
describes in its Answer are available under the current tariffs.28 PJM’s tariffs must be both clear 
and flexible to allow for a variety of fair and effective co-location solutions to emerge and 
evolve. Large loads looking to interconnect to PJM must have regulatory certainty that the 
proverbial rug will not be pulled out from under them after investing in a co-location 
arrangement. Clear tariff provisions are the basis for such regulatory certainty and will invite 
innovative solutions that bring about economic development while supporting reliability and fair 
and affordable rates for all customers. 
As discussed further below, each of the eight co-location scenarios described in PJM’s 
answer may prove viable for certain customers, depending on their capabilities and needs, and all 
eight should be accommodated. PJM and the Commission must also keep an open mind to 
 
26 PJM Answer at 32. 
27 Id. 
28 Id. at 5

11 
possibilities that may be unavailable in the current environment but could bring reliability and 
economic benefits in the future, and work to ensure sufficient flexibility within the available co-
location options to accommodate variations among customers and over time. Lack of clarity and 
flexibility in PJM’s Tariffs should not be the reason that new and innovative projects are not 
interconnected to the system.    
1. 
All Eight Co-location Options Should be Accommodated, but 
Require Additional Development 
PJM lays out eight potential co-location options, of which three are currently accounted 
for in its tariffs and five are not. It is important to recognize and preserve the three existing 
configurations, but these scenarios fail to address the new kinds of co-location arrangements that 
large loads and generators are interested in pursuing (indeed, PJM freely admits that Option 1 is 
not an example of co-location at all). The five new arrangements may all be of interest to certain 
customers depending on their specific needs and capabilities, but they lack detail. Further 
development of these options, consideration of variants, and evaluation of additional options 
through an expedient but iterative stakeholder process is necessary to provide regulatory 
certainty and proactively address the variety of co-location arrangements that will likely come 
before PJM and the Commission. PJM and the Commission should also clarify that the options 
are not mutually exclusive, and that combinations or variations of the eight listed options may be 
allowable.  
Option 1 describes an arrangement in which the load and the generator are treated 
entirely separately—they may share a contractual arrangement and a physical location, but do

12 
not share a Point of Interconnection (“POI”).29 The generator and load may or may not be 
geographically proximate, and from PJM’s perspective, there is no “co-location.” Option 2, 
similarly, is a regular network load contracted with a generator that is behind the same POI, but 
separately metered.30 These are both routine arrangements that have a limited impact on PJM’s 
system, but they ignore the drivers leading new large loads to seek out co-location agreements. 
While these options should not be removed, they also do not resolve the need for clarity 
regarding co-location.   
Option 3 reflects Behind-the-Meter Generation (“BTMG”) primarily serving the load 
rather than participating in PJM markets as a Capacity Resource.31 Existing options to pursue 
BTMG are critical to preserve. These arrangements have provided reliability benefits to the 
system and to the host load. However, this type of generation, for the most part, has not scaled up 
to accommodate large loads interconnecting to the system, and as PJM notes, there is a cap on 
BTMG opportunities with just 700 MW remaining32—a tiny quantity relative to the demand of 
new large loads in the PJM region. Given the amount of innovation in new BTMG technologies, 
this option has potential to enhance grid reliability while lowering costs for end use customers, 
but it does not address demand for co-location opportunities for new large loads.  
The three existing co-location options allowed under PJM’s current tariff therefore fail to 
anticipate the different co-location arrangements that are likely to be pursued in the PJM region. 
The availability of these existing options does not address “with sufficient clarity or consistency 
 
29 Id., at 9-10. 
30 Id., at 10-11. 
31 Id., at 11-12. 
32 Id., at 5.

13 
the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements.”33 The new 
options that PJM presents in its Answer but that are not yet accommodated in its tariff would go 
a long way toward providing regulatory certainty for new large loads and generation pursing co-
location arrangements. Developing these options proactively and generically—but with sufficient 
flexibility to accommodate individual circumstances and evolution of co-location 
opportunities—before more individual requests come before PJM and the Commission would 
not only provide clarity for large loads and generation, but also allow the Commission to resolve 
cost allocation, resource adequacy, and planning implications to ensure that co-location does not 
pose a threat to the grid or shift costs to other customers. Each of the remaining five options has 
its merits, but they all require additional development. 
Option 4 offers co-located load the opportunity to be served fully by a co-located 
resource and avoid consuming energy from the grid by using system protection facilities to 
prevent such delivery in the case that the co-located generation experiences an outage.34 
Similarly, Option 5 allows such a configuration, but gives the co-located load the option to 
receive back-up service from PJM if authorized in advance.35 Both options may be viable for 
some customers and should be accommodated in PJM’s tariff. For example, a large data center 
that brings its own backup generation or storage resource in addition to the co-located load may 
be willing to tolerate the risk of a generator outage without use of grid delivered energy as its 
“backup” supply. Specifically, some large loads, including many data centers, place such a high 
premium on reliability that they already invest in their own backup on-site generation that is not 
 
33 Show Cause Order at P 2. 
34 PJM Answer at 13-14. 
35 Id., at 14-15.

14 
producing power unless the grid—or in this case, the co-located generator—experiences an 
outage. This backup power can be configured to provide “uninterruptible power supply” to avoid 
any lag time between a grid outage and availability of the backup power supply.36 This capability 
makes Options 4 and 5 possible for large loads, which otherwise may not tolerate the risk of a 
generator outage, and also reduces the operational risks cited by PJM. Because a load customer 
selecting Options 4 or 5 is not relying on the system in the same way as a traditional network 
load, it is appropriate that PJM recognizes that such customers should not be assigned full 
network transmission charges or ancillary services and should instead be part of a new rate 
design. This rate design must be carefully discussed by stakeholders and designed with flexibility 
to accommodate different co-location arrangements and to allow large load customers that want 
additional services to have the option to take some services from PJM. Consideration of these 
options should also consider FERC jurisdiction over wholesale energy, and fairness to existing 
customers that have paid for the interconnecting transmission grid.    
Option 6 lays out the opportunity for co-located loads to “Bring Your Own Generation” 
(“BYOG”), which PJM says could be either new or existing generation, and could be either 
physically co-located or have only a contractual connection to the load.37 The opportunity for 
large loads to bring their own new generation to the system is particularly promising as it would 
directly address the root causes of co-location while effectively zeroing out the new load’s 
impact on resource adequacy. This is especially helpful in regions like PJM that are facing 
resource adequacy issues and capacity shortfalls. It is promising that PJM expresses a 
 
36 AI Data Centers Need Huge Power-Backup Systems (July 30, 2024), available at 
https://www.eetimes.com/unintended-consequences-ai-data-centers-need-huge-power-backup-systems/.  
37 PJM Answer at 16-17.

15 
willingness to accelerate interconnection for new co-located generation under this option38 but, 
as discussed further below, pathways to do so must be further defined, and much more detail is 
needed to consider and implement this solution. While PJM is open to exploring expedited 
generator interconnection under Option 6, it does not appear that this option contemplates 
opportunities to accelerate load interconnection, as PJM states that transmission system upgrades 
would employ the currently applicable Attachment M-3 Process.39  
PJM’s Option 6 does not address the different variants of BYOG, which would have 
different system impact and cost allocation implications. For example, whether the generation is 
new or existing, the choice to be physically co-located versus contractually “co-located,” and the 
nature of the physical co-location (i.e., is the load being served only by the co-located generator, 
with protections in place to prevent delivery of system energy) would impact the customer’s net 
load obligation and the impact to the system, as well as the needed upgrades to the transmission 
system. As mentioned above, speed to market is key for large loads, and options to expedite 
interconnection of both new load and new generation would benefit the customers and the 
system. In fact, these arrangements are already being considered in state proceedings and at the 
RTO/ISO level.40         
 
38 Id., at 17. 
39 Id. 
40 Application of Nevada Power Company filed under Advice Letter No. 547, to implement Clean Transition Tariff 
Schedule No. CTT to allow eligible customers to receive bundled electric service from new clean energy resources.  
Utility Commission of Nevada, Docket No. 24-05022 Order Approving Stipulation (March 11, 2025). Additionally 
the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (“MISO”) has an open stakeholder process “Market Participation 
and Registration of Co-Located Load and Generation (behind the same POI) PAC-2024-4” 
(https://www.misoenergy.org/engage/MISO-Dashboard/market-participation-and-registration-of-co-located-load-
and-generation-behind-the-same-poi/).

16 
Under Option 7, the load is not backed by capacity on the PJM system during a 
transitional period until additional capacity can be brought online, and the customer agrees to 
curtail load during events that cause reliability shortages.41 Under this option, the load can use 
on-site generation in lieu of reducing usage. While this option will likely not work for large loads 
that are inflexible or lack backup generation, it may be attractive for those that are able to curtail 
their use of grid-delivered energy. For such customers, this option offers a mutually beneficial 
arrangement: the customer does not contribute to the need for additional capacity, and in return 
avoids capacity payments. Load flexibility can also prevent the need for costly and time-
consuming upgrades to the transmission system, but this does not appear to be contemplated in 
the option, and must also be reflected in planning processes, as discussed below. A recent study 
on Virginia’s data center load growth found “[f]lexibility in load is generally expected to offset 
the need for capacity additions in a system, which could help mitigate the pressure of rapid 
resource and transmission expansion.”42 These potential iterations and/or enhancements to 
Option 7 warrant further stakeholder discussion.    
One possible adaptation of PJM’s Options 6 and 7 is brought up in the Response of 
Enchanted Rock, LLC in this proceeding. This variation lies between full isolation from the grid 
and full integration with the system. Enchanted Rock’s variation co-locates load with 
dispatchable generation to allow for load flexibility and use of as-available transmission service 
until necessary transmission upgrades make it possible for the load to fully integrate into the 
 
41 PJM Answer at 18-19. 
42 Patel, K., K. Steinberger, A. DeBenedictis, M. Wu, J. Blair, P. Picciano, and P. Oporto, et al. 2024. Virginia Data 
Center Study: Electric Infrastructure and Customer Rate Impact. San Francisco: Energy and Environmental 
Economics, Inc. https:// jlarc.virginia.gov/pdfs/presentations/JLARC%20Virginia%20Data%20Center%20 
Study_FINAL_12-09-2024.pdf.

17 
system.43 This would allow for faster interconnection for load that brings its own generation and 
has the ability to be flexible. New innovations such as this demonstrate the need for further 
stakeholder discussion, and flexibility in any tariff changes.   
Option 8 is also promising in that it recognizes and incentivizes the benefits large load 
can bring to the grid by allowing a large load to participate in PJM’s demand response (“DR”) 
program, also allowing load to utilize back-up generation to serve its demand.  This incentivizes 
valuable demand flexibility by providing a revenue stream through DR capacity payments. A 
recent study by the Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability at Duke 
University found that if large loads in PJM were curtailed only 0.25% of the time, that demand 
response could add 13.3 GW of new load with minimal capacity investment.44 PJM suggests that 
loosening federal or state emission restrictions impacting use of back-up generation may 
facilitate use of this option.45 However, there are ample resource types capable of serving co-
located loads under this arrangement without making such changes. Finally, as with the other 
options, it is important to consider these as alternative options and not requirements for 
interconnecting with the system.   
C. Transmission, Ancillary, and Other Wholesale Service Charges for Co-Location 
Should Reflect Cost Causation Principles  
All loads, including co-located loads, should pay for the transmission service, ancillary 
services, and other wholesale services they use, according to cost causation principles. Co-
 
43 “Response of Enchanted Rock, LLC” FERC Docket Nos. EL25-49, AD24-11, EL25-20, at pages 7-8.  
44 Norris, T. H., T. Profeta, D. Patino-Echeverri, and A. Cowie-Haskell. 2025. Rethinking Load Growth: Assessing 
the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems. NI R 25-01. Durham, NC: Nicholas 
Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability, Duke University at page 4. 
https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/publications/rethinking-load-growth  
45 PJM Answer at 20.

18 
location is a solution to enable speed to market and to incentivize arrangements that bring benefit 
to both the grid and the co-located load, but should not be a pathway to avoid or shift costs. 
Likewise, because of the benefits that some co-located load arrangements bring to the system, 
loads that pursue co-location should not be charged for services they do not use.  
In its Answer, PJM states that it will engage with stakeholders and Transmission Owners 
to work through questions about costs imposed on the system by the co-location agreements 
listed in its Answer.46 However, PJM appears to have predetermined that that six of the eight co-
location options it defines should be considered network load and assigned full Network 
Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”), without having explored in detail the nuances and 
different approaches that might be taken under the five scenarios that are not currently available 
in its Tariff. A new and innovative co-location arrangement should not be thrown into a bucket 
with a list of assigned charges. Instead, any rules should be flexible based on the arrangements 
and abide by the cost causation principle.47 As mentioned above, large load customers are 
exploring co-location agreements due to inefficiencies in the market, and many would prefer to 
be network load. But if these customers are investing in a co-location arrangement that avoids or 
reduces their use of transmission and wholesale services, they should also avoid the associated 
costs. PJM does recognize that some Options (i.e., Options 4 and 5) may avoid some network 
charges, but does not define how a “new rate design” would be developed, nor how flexible it 
 
46 PJM Answer at 38 
47 “FERC must ensure that rates are just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory, which requires that costs be 
allocated to those who cause them to be incurred and who benefit from them” (Illinois Commerce Commission v. 
FERC, 576 F. 3d 470, at pages 476-477 (7th Cir.).

19 
would be. PJM and the Commission should also confirm that the options are not all mutually 
exclusive.         
With respect to ancillary services, both PJM and the Transmission Owners explain that 
co-located loads utilize a range of ancillary services. PJM notes that “[t]he load and generator are 
benefiting from ancillary services (including but not limited to black start).”48 The Transmission 
Owners argue that co-located load use of ancillary services should be treated as any other load.49 
Ultimately, when large co-located loads come online, they will use some ancillary and other 
wholesale services, and should pay for the services as any customer would. Similarly, co-located 
loads should be compensated for any ancillary services their connections provide.  
D. Interconnection Procedures and Cost Allocation Must be Adapted and Clarified, 
Especially to Expedite New Generation Under BYOG 
Loads and generators pursuing co-location arrangements need clarity as to how these 
arrangements will be studied, and how those studies will be evaluated. There must be a level of 
uniformity and detail outlining study requirements to ensure regulatory certainty for large loads 
and new generation and storage resources seeking to serve large loads. This level of uniformity is 
currently lacking in PJM’s interconnection procedures and cost allocation methodology, 
particularly with respect to some of the new options PJM has outlined that are not yet 
accommodated in its tariffs.  
 With respect to retail load integration, PJM appropriately recognizes that states have 
jurisdiction over interconnection of retail loads.50 However, it is important to recognize that PJM 
 
48 PJM Answer at 42. 
49 Answer of Transmission Owners, at 13. 
50 PJM Answer at 48.

20 
will still need to play a critical role. As the regional planning authority, PJM must ensure its 
Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (“RTEP”) reliably and accurately accounts for new load 
additions to meet NERC Transmission Planning (“TPL”) standards—especially given the MW 
scale of recent interconnection requests. To that end, PJM should work collaboratively with 
Transmission Owners and large load stakeholders via an Issue Charge/Problem Statement to 
develop a standardized interconnection process. This process should include clear tracking of 
interconnection request statuses, associated financial commitments, and consistent treatment 
across projects, as discussed further below. 
With respect to interconnection of new generation to serve co-located load, guidance is 
needed to develop expedited interconnection processes for new generation resources brought 
online under the BYOG option (Option 6).51 PJM acknowledges that Tariff revisions would be 
required “for purposes of enhancing PJM’s existing provisional interconnection service construct 
or facilitating options to accelerate interconnection studies of new generation proposed as part of 
this option.”52 PJM states that it ”awaits Commission guidance on New Option 6 and any 
guidance on enhancing the transparency of the necessary study process,” but argues that a 
separate study process beyond the necessary study process or the existing interconnection queue 
is not needed. United agrees that Commission guidance is needed, but contents that a separate 
process may be warranted, and encourages the Commission to direct PJM to develop such tariff 
revisions, which could take the form of a pro forma co-located interconnection process and 
agreement.  
 
51 PJM Answer at 16. 
52 Id., at 18.

21 
Without an expedited process, customers seeking to bring new generation to serve their 
load under the BYOG option may be waiting several years to connect to the grid, defeating the 
purpose of this option. Further, keeping these projects waiting could cause cost allocation issues 
as well as reliability and resource adequacy concerns. There are also efficiencies, from both a 
study and a network upgrade perspective, from taking into account the intent for the new 
generation to serve new load when studying its impacts on the system. These efficiencies will 
save money and time and reduce the need for grid components that are subject to supply chain 
constraints. These efficiencies also differentiate projects interconnecting under a BYOG option 
such that a streamlined process to interconnect new generation under a BYOG arrangement is 
not unduly discriminatory. 
An expedited interconnection process to facilitate new resources brought online via the 
BYOG option must be fair, transparent, and not unduly discriminatory. The expedited process 
must not harm projects in the standard interconnection queue, and must grant equal, 
nondiscriminatory opportunities for independently developed projects to participate. For new 
generation that is physically co-located with load and not exporting to the gird, the study itself 
could be similar to the recently reformed surplus interconnection service process in PJM.53 The 
new generation would be studied according to the intent to only serve the new load, thus 
avoiding the need for new network upgrades.  
E. PJM Should Enhance its Planning and Load Forecasting Processes to More 
Consistently, Transparently, and Accurately Plan for Large Load Additions 
 
53 Order Accepting Tariff Revisions, 190 FERC ¶ 61,083.

22 
The Commission’s upmost concern is and should remain to be the reliability of the grid 
as co-located loads come online. In its response to the Commission, PJM noted that “[a]s a 
baseline, PJM does not believe any changes to capacity market rules are necessary to 
accommodate co-location arrangements.”54 United agrees that if co-location is pursued according 
to carefully developed, transparent, and flexible tariff provisions that account for the impact of 
different co-location arrangements on the grid, co-location should have “the same implications 
for resource adequacy as load that is not co-located.”55  
However, given the pace, scale, and uncertainty of new load additions, some changes to 
PJM’s forecasting and planning processes are warranted. For example, the impact of large loads 
on the transmission system should inform changes to the planning process. For example, PJM’s 
Option 7 acknowledges that some loads do not necessarily need to be studied and planned for 
firm 24/7 continuous power, which will likely trigger transmission expansions in addition to 
generation additions. If there were a way to recognize the up-front value of a load’s flexibility to 
drop from the grid in the transmission planning process and before load interconnection, loads 
can take ‘non-firm’ interruptible service and allow grid operators to control their onsite 
dispatchable backup generators and/or batteries to manage the relatively infrequent annual peaks.  
Further, improving the transparency and responsiveness of the load forecasting process 
will promote resource adequacy and reliability. Load forecasting within PJM must account for 
increased data center load, but currently there is a lack of standardization with regard to how 
large loads are folded into RTO/ISO planning processes, which leads to a lack of certainty about 
 
54 PJM Answer at 57. 
55 PJM Answer at 57.

23 
large loads that are included in the forecast. Large load customers are often seeking 
interconnections at multiple sites; many of these will materialize (multiple requests do not mean 
requests are speculative), but some will not. If we plan the system with the assumption that all 
load requests will show up, we will almost certainly over-build, potentially by a significant 
margin. This over-building will add unnecessary costs for all customers. Inflated load forecasts 
may also exaggerate concerns about imminent threats to resource adequacy and reliability that 
could result in costly or harmful emergency solutions that ultimately prove unnecessary. 
Currently, there is a lack of standardization across utilities in terms of how large load requests 
are incorporated into load forecasts passed to PJM. While PJM does take steps to vet the requests 
that it receives via transmission owners as part of its load forecasting process,56 a more 
standardized process that includes transparent mechanisms to discipline how large load additions 
should be accounted for in load forecasts would increase the responsiveness of the planning 
process and thus ensure reliability for consumers. 
PJM should therefore require reasonable requirements as part of its own load forecast 
verification process that are consistent across Transmission Owners. These could include 
requiring large loads to make reasonable financial commitments that increase by stage, along 
with some level of site control or exclusivity. Following the November 1, 2024, technical 
conference, multiple commenters suggested how such requirements could be developed and 
adopted.57 This topic warrants further Commission guidance and discussion in the stakeholder 
process among PJM, transmission owners, large load customers, states, and other stakeholders. 
 
56 See comments of Stu Bressler, Nov. 1, 2024 Technical Conference in Docket No. AD24-11, Transcript at 28. 
57 Post-Conference Comments of the Clean Energy Buyers Alliance in AD24-11, at 13-15; Post-Conference 
Comments of Google LLC in AD24-11, at 7-8.

24 
Further, PJM must align its internal M3 Supplemental process for load interconnections with its 
annual load forecast, which underpins regional transmission planning and resource adequacy 
needs. This alignment would provide a level of standardization and uniformity that is currently 
lacking in the load forecasting process. It is of the utmost importance for PJM to establish clear 
processes at the RTO level and financial commitments tied to transmission charges to ensure 
consistent treatment for all load requests. 
Overall, resource adequacy is a concern driven by load growth, not co-location. Co-
location, if carefully managed, does not on balance undermine resource adequacy. But 
maintaining resource adequacy requires accurately accounting for new load seeking to enter the 
system. 
F. Other Considerations 
Much of the discussion regarding co-located loads is focused on the challenges and the 
need to avoid adverse impacts, but co-location also has the potential to bring various benefits to 
the grid. Many co-located loads can provide demand response and other services to benefit the 
transmission system and should be compensated for those services, as contemplated by PJM’s 
Option 8. Any load that brings its own backup (as many data centers do) in addition to co-located 
generation brings less risk to the system. Further, loads that bring with them new generating 
resources via the BYOG option are effectively zeroing out their impact on the system, helping to 
resolve some the resource adequacy concerns and reducing necessary network upgrades. In 
addition to backup generation, behind the meter generation should be utilized, and compensated, 
to help resource adequacy and reliability. 
Ultimately, not all co-location arrangements are equal and should thus not be treated as 
such. Any tariff changes PJM must make, while increasing standardization of the process, must

25 
also allow for maximum flexibility to allow for new technologies. A standardized process can 
still exist with a level of flexibility that protects reliability and resource adequacy.  
PJM must also consider the increasing national security concerns as critical loads such as 
large data centers rely on reliable access to electricity. As data centers expand and grow quickly 
across the nation, protecting the physical security and cybersecurity of the grid is a national 
security imperative. As PJM addresses tariff changes to improve co-location growth and address 
reliability concerns, PJM must also continue to protect the grid and ensure national security.   
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
For the reasons above, Advanced Energy United respectfully requests that the 
Commission consider these comments and rule expeditiously to reduce regulatory uncertainty 
and allow large loads and new generation to enter the markets.   
Respectfully submitted this 23rd day of April 2025.
